L2: # host/bootstrap.sh — CORE layer, step 1: turn a fresh VPS into the Codery host.
L3: #
L4: # Usage:  sudo ./bootstrap.sh /path/to/secrets.env

L6: # Idempotent: safe to re-run; each step checks before acting and prints a

L10: SECRETS="${1:?usage: sudo ./bootstrap.sh <secrets.env>}"
L11: [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ] || { echo "run as root" >&2; exit 1; }
L12: [ -f "$SECRETS" ] || { echo "secrets file not found: $SECRETS" >&2; exit 1; }

L18: fi

L20: apt-get install -y -qq supervisor jq >/dev/null

L24: SYSCTL_CONF=/etc/sysctl.d/99-tailnet-binds.conf

# Codery — Infrastructure Reference

This file is loaded automatically by Claude Code and compatible agents (as
AGENTS.md). Read it before making any changes to this repo.

> **REV3 (2026-11-10) — three-layer layout.** Codery is an OS for developers:
> **core** (Dockhand, Zoraxy, Tailscale, host layer) · **tools** (paseo, apps,
> playwright, opendesign, dbgate — opt-in via compose profiles) · **projects**
> (your applications — one stack per project repo). The codery-ci binary is disabled
> on the host (revert path retained); routing is Zoraxy, stacks run under
> Dockhand. Fresh installs: `RUNBOOK.md`. Instance-specific history and
> design records live in your private deployment overlay, not in this repo.

## What This Repo Is

**Identity & push rules.** This checkout is the **public Codery repo** — push
only to `CoderyOSS/Codery` (`github-push <branch> CoderyOSS/Codery`), and
verify pushes with `git ls-remote https://github.com/CoderyOSS/Codery.git
<ref>` — always against the URL, never against a local remote. Instance-
specific work (deployment inventory, personal projects) belongs in a separate
private instance repo with its own checkout — never here. The bundled
`github-push` never modifies git remote configuration (it pushes to an
explicit URL); if you ever find a remote pointing at the wrong repo, fix it
with `git remote set-url`.

**Extension points.** Everything deployment-specific lives outside Codery's
source tree: hosted projects in `/opt/codery/projects` (bind-mounted into the
tool containers), stack configuration in `/opt/codery/stacks/<name>/.env`.
Those paths are deployment conventions, not product source — a fork is never
needed to run your own instance.

- **Stack definitions** — `stacks/core/` (dockhand, zoraxy) and
  `stacks/tools/devtools/`; canonical mirrors of the deployed copies in
  `/opt/codery/stacks/`. Never let them diverge: repo = record, stacks dir =
  runtime truth.
- **Image builds** — `images/{apps,paseo,opendesign}`; core runs stock
  upstream images, tools are Codery-built. Provenance identifies the layer.
- **Host layer** — `host/`: supervisor confs, tailscale/dns/backup scripts,
  `bootstrap.sh` (fresh-VPS prep), `templates/env.example` (secrets contract).
- **Docs** — `RUNBOOK.md` (agent bootstrap), `SETUP.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`,
  `docs/` (guides, incidents, historical runbooks, specs).
- **Agent config** — `images/paseo/opencode-config/` is the LIVE config for
  the paseo container (bind-mounted).

## The Three Layers (do not cross them)

| Layer | Members | Defined in | State lives in |
|---|---|---|---|
| Core | dockhand, zoraxy, tailscale, host layer | `stacks/core/`, `host/` | named volumes + host config |
| Tools | paseo, apps, playwright, opendesign, dbgate | `stacks/tools/devtools/`, `images/` | `/opt/codery/data/<tool>` + volumes |
| Projects | your applications | project repos (compose at repo root) | project volumes |

Rules:

1. Management/routing/perimeter → core. Developer-facing → tools.
   App-specific → project stack. No exceptions.
2. Secrets: core + tools share `/opt/codery/.env` (0600). Project secrets
   never leave the project repo.
3. Access flows downward: core manages everything; tools see projects;
   projects see only themselves.
4. Tools are opt-in: `COMPOSE_PROFILES` in the stack `.env` (`browser`,
   `design`, `db`). Base (paseo + apps) is always on; consumers degrade
   gracefully.

## Runtime Map

| Layer | Runs | Managed by |
|---|---|---|
| Router | **Zoraxy** (tailnet-IP `:443/:80`, mgmt `:8000`) — wildcard TLS via Cloudflare DNS-01, vhosts, uptime monitor | Zoraxy UI/API (Rob); agents request, never edit |
| Stacks | **Dockhand**: `devtools` + one stack per project — dockhand itself is host-side compose, never self-registered | Dockhand UI/API + `dockhand.*` agent MCP |
| Host | Tailscale, supervisord (dns-update, tailscale), sysctl tailnet binds | `host/` + RUNBOOK |

**Network fabric**: `codery-net` (external). Every stack attaches; Zoraxy
proxies by container name — HTTP services need no host port publishes.

**Host publishes** (tailnet-IP or loopback only, never public): paseo
`127.0.0.1:6767` + `:2222`; apps `:3333`, `:61000/udp`, `127.0.0.1:8080`
(transition-only); opendesign `127.0.0.1:7456`; dockhand `127.0.0.1:23000`;
zoraxy `${TAILNET_IP}:443/:80/:8000`. Sysctl `net.ipv4.ip_nonlocal_bind=1`
lets these bind before tailscale0 exists.

## Common Operations

| Situation | Action |
|---|---|
| Add/change a stack service | Edit stack compose (repo + `/opt/codery/stacks/`) → Dockhand **Deploy** |
| Add a subdomain | Zoraxy UI → proxy host (subdomain → `container:port`) |
| Container down / logs / restart | Dockhand UI or `dockhand.*` MCP |
| Enable/disable a tool | Edit `COMPOSE_PROFILES` in the stack `.env` → Deploy |
| Install a dev tool | `ssh gem@apps`, then in `~/projects/Codery/images/apps-v2`: `devbox add <pkg> && devbox install` (installs into `/nix` volume, no sudo; commit the `devbox.json`+`devbox.lock` change — `add` alone doesn't refresh the live profile, `install` does) |
| Deploy dockhand itself | host-side only: `docker compose -f /opt/codery/stacks/dockhand/compose.yml up -d` |
| Host unhealthy | `/usr/local/bin/codery-triage` (`--json` for machines) |
| Full backup | `/usr/local/bin/codery-backup.sh` → `/opt/codery/backups/` |
| Router lockout | tailnet SSH is independent: `ssh -L 23000:127.0.0.1:23000` → Dockhand UI on localhost |
| Re-enable codery-ci (revert) | retained on the host: disabled supervisor programs + `/opt/codery/state/` (see your instance docs) |

## SSH Access

| Path | Command | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Operator → paseo | `ssh -p 2222 paseo@<tailnet-ip>` | keys in `/opt/codery/ssh/authorized_keys` |
| Operator → apps | `ssh -p 3333 gem@<tailnet-ip>` | mosh via `:61000/udp` |
| paseo → apps | `ssh gem@apps` | codery-net alias; agent-to-apps key |
| Zoraxy mgmt UI | `http://<tailnet-ip>:8000` | browser only |

SSH host keys are persistent (named volumes) — fingerprints survive recreates.

## Host Environment

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `/opt/codery/.env` | THE secrets file (0600 root; sudo-only from apps) |
| `/opt/codery/stacks/` | infra stack dirs — Dockhand-deployed, gem-writable |
| `/opt/codery/projects/` | shared projects tree (paseo `/workspace`, apps `/home/gem/projects`) |
| `/opt/codery/data/` | tool service data (opencode, opendesign, dbgate) |
| `/opt/codery/{ssh,state,backups}/` | keys · disabled codery retainers · backups |
| `/run/tailscale.ip` | host tailnet IP (stack `.env` TAILNET_IP) |

Host memory: 16 GiB RAM, 4 GiB swap (swap use is normal). Watch `free -m` and
the OOM counter before big builds.

## Disabled Codery (revert path)

Supervisor programs `codery-ci`, `codery-ci-mcp`, `caddy`: stopped +
`autostart=false`; state retained on the host (`/opt/codery/state/`,
`codery.db`, binary, images). Rust source is recoverable from git history
(pre-`migration/runtime-ops`). Re-enable steps live in your instance docs
(the retained host state documents the exact programs and paths).

## Workflows (.github/workflows)

Images build **locally on the VPS host** — no GitHub CI for images:

    docker build -t codery-apps:$(date +%Y%m%d) /opt/codery/projects/Codery/images/apps

then point the stack `.env` (`APPS_IMAGE`/`PASEO_IMAGE`) at the new tag and
Deploy. `diagnose.yml` — host-repair path. (The old `release-apps.yml`
ghcr/tag-push pipeline was removed 2026-11-12.)

## Sensitive Files — Do Not Read or Expose

NEVER read, cat, print, or include their contents in output:

- `.env`, `*.env.*` — API keys, tokens, credentials
- `/run/secrets/*` — GitHub App PEM key (bind-mounted)
- `~/.ssh/*`, `/opt/codery/ssh/agent-to-apps` — private keys
- `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json` — provider API keys
- `*.pem`, `*.key` — any private key files

Check existence only (`test -f`), never read contents.

# AI Agent Instructions — Paseo container

You are a coding agent inside the Codery (github.com/CoderyOSS/Codery) **paseo
container** on the VPS, spawned by the Paseo daemon (the iPad Paseo app talks
to this daemon; it owns the agent processes it launches). You have MCPs for
container stack operations (`dockhand`), GitHub App operations (`github-app`),
and — if deployed — browser automation (`playwright`; it is an opt-in tool:
check `dockhand_stack_ps` before assuming browser tools exist).

## Your Capabilities

- **Full bash/shell access** — run any command in the terminal
- **File access** — read/write under `/workspace/` (bind-mounted from host
  `/opt/codery/projects` — the shared projects tree)
- **GitHub access** — GitHub App auth via the git credential helper. **Do not
  say you lack GitHub access** — you have it. There is no `gh` CLI in this
  image; for API calls mint a token with `github-app-token` and use `curl`.
- **Code push** — use `github-push` to push branches and tags (never
  `git push` directly)

Verify GitHub auth:
```bash
git ls-remote https://github.com/CoderyOSS/Codery HEAD && echo AUTH-OK
```

## Environment

Host runs Zoraxy (routing), Tailscale (the perimeter), supervisord, and

## Bun bcrypt pitfall: `Bun.password.verify` silently fails on `$2a$`/`$2y$` hashes

`Bun.password.verify()` (confirmed on Bun 1.2.13, linux/x64) returns `false` — it does
not throw — for every bcrypt hash prefixed `$2a$` or `$2y$`, at any cost factor. Only
`$2b$` hashes verify. Since `Bun.password.hash()` itself emits `$2b$`, Bun-internal
hash→verify roundtrips work and mask the bug; but hashes from Go
(`golang.org/x/crypto/bcrypt`, `caddy hash-password`), PHP `password_hash()`,
`htpasswd -B`, OpenBSD, passlib, etc. are usually `$2a$`/`$2y$` and will ALWAYS fail
verification under Bun — indistinguishably from a wrong password.

Workaround — normalize the prefix before verifying (2a/2b/2y are algorithmically
identical for normal-length passwords):

    const ok = await Bun.password.verify(pw, hash.replace(/^\$2[ay]\$/, "$2b$"));

Never assume "verify returned false ⇒ password wrong" under Bun; check the hash prefix
first, and never write bcrypt test fixtures using only `Bun.password.hash()` output.

# /graphify

Turn any folder of files into a navigable knowledge graph with community detection, an honest audit trail, and three outputs: interactive HTML, GraphRAG-ready JSON, and a plain-language GRAPH_REPORT.md.

## Usage

```
/graphify                                             # full pipeline on current directory (HTML viz; add --obsidian for a vault)
/graphify <path>                                      # full pipeline on specific path
/graphify https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>           # clone repo then run full pipeline on it
/graphify https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> --branch <branch>  # clone a specific branch
/graphify <url1> <url2> ...                           # clone multiple repos, build each, merge into one cross-repo graph
/graphify <path> --mode deep                          # thorough extraction, richer INFERRED edges
/graphify <path> --update                             # incremental - re-extract only new/changed files
/graphify <path> --directed                            # build directed graph (preserves edge direction: source→target)
/graphify <path> --whisper-model medium                # use a larger Whisper model for better transcription accuracy
/graphify <path> --cluster-only                       # rerun clustering on existing graph
/graphify <path> --no-viz                             # skip visualization, just report + JSON
/graphify <path> --html                               # (HTML is generated by default - this flag is a no-op)
/graphify <path> --svg                                # also export graph.svg (embeds in Notion, GitHub)
/graphify <path> --graphml                            # export graph.graphml (Gephi, yEd)
/graphify <path> --neo4j                              # generate graphify-out/cypher.txt for Neo4j
/graphify <path> --neo4j-push bolt://localhost:7687   # push directly to Neo4j
/graphify <path> --falkordb                           # generate graphify-out/cypher.txt for FalkorDB
/graphify <path> --falkordb-push falkordb://localhost:6379   # push directly to FalkorDB
/graphify <path> --mcp                                # start MCP stdio server for agent access
/graphify <path> --watch                              # watch folder, auto-rebuild on code changes (no LLM needed)
/graphify <path> --wiki                               # build agent-crawlable wiki (index.md + one article per community)
/graphify <path> --obsidian --obsidian-dir ~/vaults/my-project  # write vault to custom path (e.g. existing vault)
/graphify add <url>                                   # fetch URL, save to ./raw, update graph
/graphify add <url> --author "Name"                   # tag who wrote it
/graphify add <url> --contributor "Name"              # tag who added it to the corpus
/graphify query "<question>"                          # BFS traversal - broad context
/graphify query "<question>" --dfs                    # DFS - trace a specific path

/graphify path "AuthModule" "Database"                # shortest path between two concepts

Drop any folder of code, docs, papers, images, or video into graphify and get a queryable knowledge graph. Persistent across sessions, honest audit trail (EXTRACTED/INFERRED/AMBIGUOUS), community detection surfaces cross-document connections you wouldn't think to ask about.

```

│  PROJECTS — your code                                            │

├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

- **Core** runs stock upstream images; **tools** are Codery-built (`images/`).

- **Access flows downward**: core manages everything, tools see projects,

- **Tools are opt-in** — the `COMPOSE_PROFILES` list in a stack's `.env`
  decides what deploys; consumers degrade gracefully without them.

# Apps Container — Nix Toolchains + s6-overlay

Apps container uses [Nix](https://nixos.org) for reproducible, declarative toolchains and
[s6-overlay](https://github.com/just-containers/s6-overlay) for process supervision.
All packages come from a pinned nixpkgs revision; NvChad is cloned at a pinned commit.

## Files

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `images/apps/Dockerfile` | `nixos/nix` base image, `nix profile install` + `home-manager switch` + s6-overlay |
| `images/apps/flake.nix` | System profile (Rust, Elixir, Bun, gcc, nvim, sshd, infra) |
| `images/apps/home.nix` | home-manager module for `gem` — neovim + treesitter parsers |
| `images/apps/s6-overlay/` | s6-rc service definitions (ssh-agent, sshd, tmux, oneshots) |
| `images/apps/sshd_config` | OpenSSH server config |

## Process supervision (s6-overlay)

s6-overlay is PID 1. Services are defined as s6-rc source definition
directories under `images/apps/s6-overlay/s6-rc.d/` and included in the `user` bundle.

| Service | Type | Description |
|---------|------|-------------|
| `ssh-host-keys` | oneshot | `ssh-keygen -A` — generates host keys on first boot |
| `sshd` | longrun | `/usr/sbin/sshd -D -e` — depends on `ssh-host-keys` |
| `ssh-agent` | longrun | `ssh-agent -a /tmp/ssh-agent.sock -d` |
| `ssh-agent-keys` | oneshot | Loads SSH keys — depends on `ssh-agent` |
| `nginx-placeholder` | oneshot | Writes fallback config if bind mount missing |
| `nginx` | longrun | `nginx -c /etc/nginx/nginx.conf` — depends on `nginx-placeholder` |

All services depend on s6-overlay's `base` bundle (system readiness). Dependencies enforce
ordering — no race conditions between sshd and host key generation.

To add a new static service (baked into the image), add an s6-rc directory, an empty file
in `user-bundles.d/user/contents.d/`, and the Dockerfile COPY will pick it up.

# GitAuthGate (gag)

GitHub auth gate for agent-driven git and API access: a machine account's
PAT is custodied (AES-GCM-encrypted at rest), agents proxy git and API
traffic through gate, and the policy engine decides per action class —
`allow`, `deny`, or `approve` (Telegram hold; fail-closed without a bot).

Single static musl binary; runtime is `scratch` (no shell, no git) running
as uid 65532. State lives in `/data` (`gate.db` + `audit.jsonl`), owned by
the image itself — a fresh named volume auto-seeds with correct ownership
on first boot.

     then `docker compose up -d`.
4. **First run**: browse to the gate page through your reverse proxy route
   (Zoraxy on Codery hosts: `gag.<domain>` → `gitauthgate:8080`) and follow
   the rendered instructions — `/setup/token` stores the machine account's
   PAT, encrypted with `GATE_TOKEN_ENC_KEY` into `/data/gate.db`.

From then on, agents use gate as their GitHub origin:
`https://<gate-host>/git/<owner>/<repo>` (git smart HTTP) and
`/api/v3/...` (API proxy). `/whoami` shows the authenticated sphere.

## Configuration

- **Policy** (`policy.toml`, bind-mounted read-only): per-class decisions
  for `push`, `force-push`, `branch-delete`, `tag-delete` plus `[api]`
  mutations; `[repos."owner/repo"]` overrides inherit `[defaults]`.
  Unset = deny. Non-own-sphere mutations always require approval.
- **Cadences**: `GATE_*_SECS` env overrides (see `src/config.rs`); sane
  defaults, no need to set them.

## Operations

- **Upgrade**: bump the tag in the `compose.yml` `image:` line,
  `docker build -t codery-gitgate:<newtag> .`, then redeploy the stack —
  the version bump is a reviewed, in-history change.
- **Rollback**: flip `image:` back to the previous tag, redeploy.

# Codery — Architecture

What runs where, how traffic flows, and the rules that keep the system
comprehensible. For setup see [SETUP.md](SETUP.md) / [RUNBOOK.md](RUNBOOK.md);
for the agent contract see [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md).

## The layers

| Layer | Members | Defined in | Deployed by | State |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Core** | Dockhand, Zoraxy, Tailscale, host layer | `stacks/core/`, `host/` | host-side compose / Dockhand | `codery-dockhand-data`, `zoraxy_state` volumes, host config |
| **Tools** | paseo, apps, playwright, opendesign, dbgate | `stacks/tools/devtools/`, `images/` | Dockhand (`devtools` stack) | `/opt/codery/data/*` + named volumes |
| **Projects** | your applications | project repos (compose in project root) | Dockhand (per-project stacks) | project-scoped volumes |

**Extension points** (why no fork is ever needed): hosted projects live in
`/opt/codery/projects` — outside this source tree; per-stack configuration
lives in `/opt/codery/stacks/<name>/.env` (images, `TAILNET_IP`,
`COMPOSE_PROFILES`, tokens). A deployment = Codery product + external config.

**Layer tests** (apply before adding anything):

- management / routing / perimeter → **core** — stock upstream image, no custom
  builds
- developer-facing tool → **tools** — Codery-built image, opt-in via
  `COMPOSE_PROFILES`
- app-specific → **project stack** — lives in the project repo, never in
  `images/` or `/opt/codery/data`

## Host layout (`/opt/codery/`)

```
.env          THE secrets file (0600) — every core/tool stack reads it
stacks/       infra stack dirs: dockhand/, zoraxy/, devtools/ (+ stack .envs)
projects/     project repos — their compose stacks live at each repo root
data/         tool service data: opencode/, opendesign/, dbgate/
ssh/          authorized_keys + agent-to-apps keypair
state/        disabled codery-ci retainers (revert path only)
backups/      codery-backup.sh output
```

Full tree documentation: `/opt/codery/README.md` on the host.

## Traffic flow

```
iPad / dev machines (tailnet)
   │  *.<your-domain> → tailscale IP
   ▼
Zoraxy :443 (wildcard TLS, Cloudflare DNS-01)
   │  proxy-host → codery-net container names (no host ports for HTTP)
   ▼
paseo:6767 · apps:<port> · opendesign:7456 · dbgate:3000
webapp:3000 · api:8000 · dockhand:3000 — whatever your projects run
```

Only SSH, mosh, and transition publishes touch host ports
(`:2222 paseo ssh`, `:3333/:61000 apps`, `:8080 apps nginx — transition-only`,
`:23000 dockhand`, Zoraxy on the tailnet IP). Everything HTTP is name-based
on `codery-net`.

## Boot order & invariants

1. tailscale (host daemon) → 2. docker → 3. stacks. Host sysctl
   `net.ipv4.ip_nonlocal_bind=1` lets tailnet-IP binds succeed before
   tailscale0 exists (`/etc/sysctl.d/99-tailnet-binds.conf`).

Invariants that must never be violated:

- `codery-dockhand-data` volume is never renamed (holds all `dh_` tokens)
- dockhand is never deployed by Dockhand itself (lockout foot-gun) — host-side
  compose only
- `env_file: /opt/codery/.env` requires the file to be mounted into the
  dockhand container (compose resolves env_file client-side)
- container/host names are DNS: Zoraxy upstreams are codery-net names; renaming
  a container breaks routes unless the alias moves with it

## Visibility & permissions

| Consumer | Sees | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| apps (operator terminal) | full `/opt/codery` | `stacks/` as gem; everything else via sudo (secrets 0600) |
| paseo agents | `/opt/codery/{stacks,data}` | read-only |
| projects | their own tree | their own volumes |

## Opt-in tools

`COMPOSE_PROFILES` in the devtools stack `.env` is the inclusion list:
`browser` (playwright), `design` (opendesign), `db` (dbgate). Base (paseo +
apps) is always on. Absent tools degrade gracefully — paseo browser tools fail
fast; opendesign previews error until `browser` is enabled alongside.

# RUNBOOK — Operating a Codery VPS

**Start here.** This is the operating guide for an AI agent (OpenMINIS-class)
running a Codery VPS: fresh install and bootstrap (Part I), day-to-day
operations (Part II), debugging and repair (Part III), maintenance (Part IV).

Read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) once before acting — it defines the operating
contract (layer rules, what never to touch, secrets handling, container
hygiene). This runbook is procedures; that file is rules.
Humans: [SETUP.md](SETUP.md). Architecture background: [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md).

**Non-negotiables, up front:**

- Never recreate the paseo container from within paseo (it hosts the working
  agent). Container switches only when agent sessions are idle.
- Never deploy dockhand via Dockhand itself — host-side compose only.
- The `codery-dockhand-data` volume is never renamed (it holds every `dh_` API
  token).
- Secrets live in `/opt/codery/.env` (0600). Never read or print it — check
  existence with `test -f`, never `cat`.
- Route changes happen in the Zoraxy UI/API — request them from the operator,
  never invent routing.

# Part I — Fresh install (bootstrap)

**Audience for this part:** an agent with root SSH on a fresh Ubuntu/Debian
24.x VPS, this repo cloned, and operator-staged secrets.

## Phase 0 — Contracts

**You receive:**

- root SSH to a fresh VPS (no other software assumed)
- this repo, cloned to the VPS at `/root/Codery`
- secrets staged at `/root/secrets.env` in `KEY=value` form — the key set is
  exactly [`host/templates/env.example`](host/templates/env.example). If a key
  is missing, STOP and ask the operator; do not invent values.

**You deliver:**

- a running system: Tailscale perimeter, Dockhand management plane, Zoraxy
  routing edge (wildcard TLS), the devtools stack, operator access verified
- the operator's first task after handoff: change passwords, review Zoraxy
  routes

**Operator decisions to collect before starting** (ask once):

- domain name (default: `example.com`)
- which opt-in tools to deploy: `COMPOSE_PROFILES` list (default `browser,db`)

## Phase 1 — CORE

### 1.1 Host layer

```bash
sudo bash /root/Codery/host/bootstrap.sh /root/secrets.env
```

The script is idempotent: installs docker + supervisord + tailscale, sets the
tailnet-bind sysctl, builds the `/opt/codery` tree, assembles
`/opt/codery/.env` from staged secrets, installs host scripts and supervisor
confs, brings up tailscale. Read it before running; it prints a gate line per
step.

**Gate C1:** `tailscale ip` returns an IP; `docker info` works;
`ls /opt/codery/.env /opt/codery/stacks` all exist; `cat /run/tailscale.ip`
returns the same IP.

### 1.2 Dockhand

```bash
mkdir -p /opt/codery/stacks/dockhand
cp /root/Codery/stacks/core/dockhand/compose.yml /opt/codery/stacks/dockhand/
cat > /opt/codery/stacks/dockhand/.env <<EOF
DOCKHAND_IMAGE=ghcr.io/finsys/dockhand:latest
EOF
docker compose -f /opt/codery/stacks/dockhand/compose.yml \
  --env-file /opt/codery/stacks/dockhand/.env up -d
```

First-run: open `http://<tailnet-ip>:23000`, create the admin account, mint an
API token (`dh_…`) — the operator does this or hands you credentials.

**Gate C2:** `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:23000/api/health` returns 200;
`docker ps` shows `dockhand` healthy.

### 1.3 Zoraxy + wildcard TLS

```bash
mkdir -p /opt/codery/stacks/zoraxy
cp /root/Codery/stacks/core/zoraxy/compose.yml /opt/codery/stacks/zoraxy/
echo "TAILNET_IP=$(cat /run/tailscale.ip)" > /opt/codery/stacks/zoraxy/.env
docker compose -f /opt/codery/stacks/zoraxy/compose.yml \
  --env-file /opt/codery/stacks/zoraxy/.env up -d
```

Then: `:8000` → create admin account; add wildcard cert via Cloudflare DNS-01
(`CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` from the secrets file); add proxy-hosts as services
come up (table in ARCHITECTURE.md).

**Gate C3:** `curl -sk https://<tailnet-ip>/ -H 'Host: <domain>'` answers
(with cert or default page); Zoraxy shows the tailnet upstreams healthy.

### 1.4 codery-net

```bash
docker network create codery-net
```

**Gate C4:** `docker network ls` shows `codery-net`.

## Phase 2 — TOOLS (devtools stack)

```bash
mkdir -p /opt/codery/stacks/devtools
cp /root/Codery/stacks/tools/devtools/compose.yml /opt/codery/stacks/devtools/
cat > /opt/codery/stacks/devtools/.env <<EOF
TAILNET_IP=$(cat /run/tailscale.ip)
PASEO_IMAGE=<paseo image ref>
APPS_IMAGE=<apps image ref>
OPENDESIGN_IMAGE=<opendesign image ref>   # only if design profile wanted
COMPOSE_PROFILES=<chosen list, e.g. browser,db>
SSH_DIR=/opt/codery/ssh
DOCKHAND_API_TOKEN=<dh_ token from 1.2>
DOMAIN_NAME=<operator domain>
EOF
docker compose -f /opt/codery/stacks/devtools/compose.yml \
  --env-file /opt/codery/stacks/devtools/.env up -d
```

Prefer deploying through Dockhand once it's up (register the stack from
`/opt/codery/stacks/devtools/compose.yml`) — after this phase, Dockhand owns
the stack lifecycle.

Image note: build the tools images on the host — no registry needed:

    docker build -t codery-apps:$(date +%Y%m%d) /opt/codery/projects/Codery/images/apps
    docker build -t codery-paseo:$(date +%Y%m%d) /opt/codery/projects/Codery/images/paseo

then point `APPS_IMAGE` / `PASEO_IMAGE` in the stack `.env` at those tags
(`GHCR_*` keys only matter if you instead pull prebuilt images).

**MANDATORY for every apps image deploy** (skip only on a fresh volume,
i.e. first-ever boot): the `/nix` named volume is not empty, so Docker will
NOT re-seed it from the new image. Run the store sync BEFORE pointing
`APPS_IMAGE` at the new tag and deploying:

    /opt/codery/projects/Codery/host/scripts/nix-store-sync.sh codery-apps:<tag> codery-apps-nix

Skipping this step is a known failure class (2026-11-12 incident): the
volume's store drifts from the image's store, store-referenced symlinks in
the container (`/etc/nix/nix.conf` -> `<hash>-base-system/...`, gem's
home-manager dotfiles) dangle, and shells come up with a bare sshd PATH
(`mosh`/`tooladd`/coreutils unreachable). The script does a full `cp -a`
plus in-run verification; if it reports a failure, STOP and inspect before
deploying. After deploying, verify `ssh gem@apps 'echo $PATH'` includes the
nix profile dirs and `/nix/var/nix/profiles/tools/bin`.

**Gate T1:** `docker ps` shows paseo + apps (+ profiled tools) running and
healthy. **Gate T2:** `ssh -p 2222 paseo@<tailnet-ip>` works; `ssh -p 3333
gem@<tailnet-ip>` works; mosh connects. **Gate T3:** an agent session in paseo
loads the `dockhand.*` MCP (`dockhand_list_stacks` returns the stacks).

Add Zoraxy proxy-hosts for the enabled tools (code., opendesign., dbgate. →
container:port from the compose header).

## Phase 3 — PROJECTS (pulling in your code)

Each personal project lives in its own git repo and carries its compose file
at the repo root (the Codery convention). Adding one to the instance:

1. **Clone into the shared projects tree** — `/opt/codery/projects/<name>`.
   Two paths, pick one:
   - **Via paseo (recommended for private repos):** after Phase 2 the GitHub
     App credential helper in paseo covers the configured repos. In an agent
     session: `git clone https://github.com/<you>/<project>.git
     /workspace/<project>` (paseo sees the tree at `/workspace`).
   - **As the operator:** your own machine or the apps terminal, with your
     own GitHub auth, cloning to the same path.
2. **Confirm the compose file** — `<project>/docker-compose.yml` at the root.
   No compose file means project work comes first; nothing to deploy.
3. **Attach reachable services to `codery-net`** — any service a browser,
   agent, or tool must hit declares the external `codery-net` network (the
   pattern every project compose shows). Databases conventionally join so
   dbgate and agents can reach them; purely-internal services can stay on
   the stack's default network.
4. **Secrets stay in the project** — e.g. `<project>/backend/.env`. Never
   move them into `/opt/codery/.env`. Create any non-committed env files the
   project's docs require.
5. **Register in Dockhand** — Stacks → new stack → point it at the compose
   file's absolute path (`/opt/codery/projects/<name>/docker-compose.yml`);
   Dockhand runs it from the project dir. Fill in any stack variables it
   asks for; Deploy — with *build* enabled if the compose has `build:`
   sections.
6. **Route it** (if it serves HTTP) — Zoraxy UI → proxy host
   `<name>.<domain>` → `container:port`. Wildcard TLS already covers it.
7. **Gate per project:** containers healthy in Dockhand, the route answers
   through Zoraxy with TLS, and any databases show up in dbgate.

**Updating a project later:** `git pull` in the project tree → Dockhand
Deploy. Config-hash based: only changed services recreate; enable build for
image-rebuilding projects.

## Handoff checklist

- [ ] operator changes Dockhand admin + Zoraxy admin passwords
- [ ] `host/templates/env.example` keys all present in `/opt/codery/.env`
      (0600, root-owned)
- [ ] first `codery-backup.sh` run + restore spot-check
- [ ] `ARCHITECTURE.md` read by the operator (10 minutes, saves hours)

# Part II — Day-to-day operations

| Task | Procedure |
|---|---|
| Add a project | Part I Phase 3 — clone into `/opt/codery/projects/`, register the compose in Dockhand, route in Zoraxy |
| Change a stack service | Edit the stack compose — repo copy AND `/opt/codery/stacks/<name>/compose.yml` (never let them diverge) → Dockhand **Deploy** (or `POST /api/stacks/<name>/deploy`) |
| Enable/disable a tool | Edit `COMPOSE_PROFILES` in the stack `.env` → Deploy. Removing a tool leaves its container as an orphan — remove it once in the Dockhand UI |
| Add a subdomain | Zoraxy UI → proxy host (subdomain → `container:port` on codery-net) |
| Install a dev tool | `ssh gem@apps tooladd <nixpkgs-pkg>` — persists in the `/nix` volume; manifest auto-committed to the repo |
| Deploy dockhand itself | Host-side only: `docker compose -f /opt/codery/stacks/dockhand/compose.yml --env-file /opt/codery/stacks/dockhand/.env up -d` |
| Full backup | `sudo /usr/local/bin/codery-backup.sh` → `/opt/codery/backups/` |
| Update Codery itself | `git pull` the repo (or merge upstream `main` into your private overlay), rebuild images on the host (`docker build -t codery-apps:$(date +%Y%m%d) …`), then per-stack Deploy |

**Stack-change rule:** every deploy is config-hash based — services whose
config didn't change are not recreated. If a paseo recreate is possible, do it
only with agent sessions idle.

---

# Part III — Debugging & repair

| Symptom | First moves |
|---|---|
| Container down / crash loop | Dockhand UI or `dockhand.*` MCP: `stack_ps` → `stack_logs` (tail 100) |
| Dockhand deploy fails with `env file … not found` | The stack compose references an `env_file` path the dockhand container can't see (only `/opt/codery/stacks` and `/opt/codery/projects` are mounted). Mount the missing file into dockhand or inline the values |
| Site 502 via Zoraxy | Check the upstream container is running (`stack_ps`), then the Zoraxy proxy-host target name matches the container name/alias |
| Zoraxy state lost (vhosts/certs gone) | Run `/opt/codery/stacks/zoraxy/bootstrap-state.sh` — restores admin, ACME, wildcard cert, and the vhost list |
| Router lockout | Tailnet SSH is independent: `ssh -L 23000:127.0.0.1:23000 <host>` → Dockhand UI on localhost |
| Host unhealthy | `sudo /usr/local/bin/codery-triage` (`--json` for machines); check `free -m` and OOM counter before big builds |
| Agent can't spawn / MCPs fail | paseo: never run `opencode` as root (root-owned state breaks every later session — see AGENTS.md hygiene rules). Check `~/.local/state/opencode/` ownership |
| SSH to a container fails | Publishes are native docker ports; check the stack is up, then host keys (`codery-paseo-ssh-host-keys` / `codery-apps-ssh-host-keys` volumes survive recreates) |
| Disk pressure | `docker system df`; prune dangling images only after checking Dockhand's pinned digests; `/opt/codery/backups/` is the usual grower |

**Repair rule:** one change at a time, verify, then next. If three fixes fail,
stop and question the diagnosis, not the luck.

---

# Part IV — Maintenance

| Cadence | Task |
|---|---|
| Weekly | `codery-backup.sh` (or cron); spot-check a restore monthly |
| Monthly | `docker system df` + disk check; review Zoraxy uptime monitor for flapping targets |
| Quarterly | Rotate `dh_` tokens if operators changed; re-read ARCHITECTURE.md invariants against the live system |
| On cert warnings | Wildcard auto-renews via DNS-01; if it lapses, `bootstrap-state.sh` re-obtains it |
| On Codery updates | Pull the repo, review the diff (composes + docs), then update stacks one at a time with Deploy; paseo last |

**Break-glass (full revert):** the pre-Dockhand codery-ci machinery is
disabled, not deleted — supervisor programs stopped + `autostart=false`, state
in `/opt/codery/state/`, binary/images retained. Re-enable steps live in the
instance docs of your private deployment overlay. Use only if the Dockhand/Zoraxy
end-state is unrecoverable — it is a rollback, not a repair.

# GATE-001: GitAuthGate is an opt-in tools-layer service

## Context

Codery separates core (dockhand, zoraxy, tailscale), tools (paseo, apps,
playwright, opendesign, dbgate), and projects. Tools are opt-in: each has a
compose `profile`, and users enable it by adding the profile name to
`COMPOSE_PROFILES` in the stack `.env`. Users may not want a GitHub gate;
absent tools must simply not exist and degrade nothing.

The gate exists because managing a GitHub App's credentials and per-org
permissions is clunky and the operator wants every agent action behind a
gate they control. It serves agent instances; it is developer-facing, not
infrastructure.

## Decision

GitAuthGate follows the OpenDesign placement model exactly:

- One service `gitauthgate` in `stacks/tools/devtools/compose.yml` with
  `profiles: [gag]`.
- Image built on-host from `images/gate/` (`docker build -t
  codery-gate:<date> images/gate`), selected via `GATE_IMAGE` in the stack
  `.env`.
- Attached to `codery-net` with container name/alias `gitauthgate`.
- Secrets come from `/opt/codery/.env` via the compose `env_file`; per-user
  state lives in a bind mount at `/opt/codery/data/gate`.
- Loopback port publish only (`127.0.0.1:<port>`), like opendesign.
- A Zoraxy proxy-host route `gag.<domain>` → `gitauthgate:<port>` is
  **required**, not optional: GATE-004's one-time token-intake form must be
  reachable over HTTPS by the user's browser. The user applies the route in
  the Zoraxy UI; agents request it, never create it.

**Agent env wiring** (builder check settled): compose profiles cannot
conditionally add environment to a *different* service, so the paseo
service carries gate-related vars as empty-default interpolations — e.g.
`GH_HOST: ${GATE_AGENT_HOST:-}`, `GITHUB_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN:
${GATE_AGENT_TOKEN:-}` — which the stack `.env` sets only when the `gag`
profile is enabled. `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` is set unconditionally
(harmless without the gate). Whether `gh` treats an *empty* `GH_HOST` as
unset is verified in the M1 spike; if not, the fallback is a commented
env block flipped during opt-in (documented, zero image changes). P0
wires **paseo only**; agents in the apps container are wired manually per
the setup guide. Deployment verification (spike deliverables): containers
must actually reach `gag.{domain}` (DNS + TLS from codery-net), and the
Zoraxy route's timeout must exceed the approval-hold timeout (GATE-005) —
else the hold timeout is lowered below Zoraxy's limit. Fallback when no
public URL exists: agents use the internal alias (`http://gitauthgate:<port>`,
codery-net only), setup falls back to paste-in-Telegram, and wiring
instructions are delivered over Telegram instead of `GET /`.

## Do's and Don'ts

- Do add the service and its env keys to the canonical mirror in this repo
  and to the deployed copy in `/opt/codery/stacks/` together.
- Do degrade gracefully: with the `gag` profile off, no paseo env var may
  point at a dead gate (see GATE-002/GATE-007 wiring notes).
- Don't publish the gate on a public host port or route it through Zoraxy
  to the public internet; the tailnet + codery-net boundary is assumed by
  GATE-006's threat model.
- Don't store secrets in the repo; the secrets contract lives in
  `host/templates/env.example`.

## Consequences

- Positive: one-profile opt-in; removing it leaves zero residue; multiple
  instances (one per user) are possible by stacking profiles in private
  deployments.
- Trade-off: the Zoraxy route is a manual step outside the agent's reach —
  accepted, it happens once per instance.
- Risk: users forget the route exists and the setup form 502s. Mitigation:
  the setup walkthrough (GATE-011) detects an unreachable public URL and
  says so in plain words.

## Compliance and Enforcement

Enforced by review: the compose diff must show `profiles: [gag]`, no
`0.0.0.0` port publishes, and env keys matching GATE-009.

## References

- GATE-002, GATE-004, GATE-009, GATE-011
- `stacks/tools/devtools/compose.yml` (opendesign service as the model)

# GATE-002: Remote model — canonical `origin` + `gag` remote, onboarding by instruction page

## Context

The agent's git operations must pass through the gate, but git is
convention-driven and an agent that "gets confused" must not bypass it by
habit. Two shapes were considered:

1. Transparent URL rewriting (`url.insteadOf` mapping `https://github.com/`
   to the gate). Rejected: it hides the mechanism from the user and the
   agent, breaks non-git HTTPS traffic expectations, and is one global
   config away from surprising everyone.
2. Git's native remotes: keep `origin` pointing at the real GitHub URL and
   operate through a second remote. Chosen.

The end state must be identical whether the repo was cloned from GitHub
directly (public repo) or through the gate (private repo): `origin` tracks
GitHub; only `gag` touches the gate.

## Decision

In every agent-worked repo:

```
remote origin → https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}        # canonical, pristine, no credentials
remote gag    → https://gag.{domain}/git/{owner}/{repo}  # gate URL, agent token credential
git config remote.pushDefault gag                        # plain `git push` goes through the gate
```

Enforcement layers:

1. `remote.pushDefault = gag` — the default push destination is the gate.
2. Explicit pushes to `origin` fail on their own: the agent holds no GitHub
   credential (GATE-003/GATE-004), credential prompting is disabled
   (`GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`, no credential helper for github.com), so
   GitHub answers 401 and nothing happens.
3. The instruction page (`GET /` on the gate, rendered with the live gate
   hostname and a minted-token placeholder) serves the exact copy-paste
   setup for both clone paths. No shipped `gag`/`gag init`/`gag clone`
   scripts in P0 — instructions only.

Clone paths served by the instruction page:

- **Public repo:** clone from GitHub normally, then add the `gag` remote,
  set `remote.pushDefault`, and configure commit identity (GATE-004 §8.4).
- **Private repo:** the agent cannot clone from GitHub at all (no
  credential); it clones through the gate, then converges:

  ```bash
  git clone https://agent:{token}@gag.{domain}/git/{owner}/{repo}.git
  cd repo
  git remote rename origin gag
  git remote add origin https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}.git
  git config remote.pushDefault gag
  ```

When no public URL is configured, agents use the internal codery-net alias
instead of `gag.{domain}` and the same instructions are delivered over
Telegram rather than `GET /` (GATE-001 fallback mode).

Fetches: `git fetch` on `origin` works for public repos without
credentials — read-only and accepted as unaudited (explicit user decision).
Private-repo fetches fail on `origin` and go through `git fetch gag`.
Branch tracking stays on `origin` (explicit user decision).

## Do's and Don'ts

- Do leave `origin` byte-identical to a normal clone; never rewrite its URL.
- Do include commit identity setup in the instruction page; commits are
  built client-side.
- Don't use `url.insteadOf` or any transparent rewrite.
- Don't ship helper scripts in P0; the page is the onboarding.

## Consequences

- Positive: the mechanism is visible and standard git; bypassing requires a
  deliberate act (`git push origin` plus stolen credentials that don't
  exist); both clone paths converge.
- Trade-off: the agent token sits in the `gag` remote URL (visible in
  `git remote -v`) — accepted for P0; tokens are revocable instantly
  (GATE-003) and scoped to gate-only power.
- Risk: an agent pushes explicitly to `origin`. It fails closed — no
  credential exists to make it succeed.

## Compliance and Enforcement

Review-verified: instruction page content matches this ADR; `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`
set in the agent environment wiring; no `insteadOf` anywhere in shipped config.

## References

- GATE-003 (agent auth), GATE-004 (commit identity), GATE-007 (API env)

# GATE-003: Agent-to-gate authentication — revocable bearer tokens

## Context

The agent must authenticate to the gate, but the credential it holds must be
worthless against `github.com` directly — otherwise a prompt-injected agent
bypasses the gate entirely. Candidates:

- **SSH keys** (traditional): key in `~/.ssh`, no secret in URLs, but
  requires an SSH server stack (russh), a Telegram-approved pubkey
  enrollment flow (an open "send pubkey" endpoint is an auth bypass), and
  host-key bootstrap friction in non-interactive agent sessions.
- **Bearer token over the gate's existing HTTPS listener**: zero new
  protocol, git's native transport, credential machinery the agent already
  knows.

## Decision

The gate issues **opaque random bearer tokens** to agents:

- Minted and revoked over Telegram: `/token mint <name>`, `/token revoke <name>`
  (GATE-006). Revocation takes effect on the next request — every request
  validates the token.
- Stored **hashed** (SHA-256) in SQLite with a name and created/last-used
  timestamps; the raw token exists only at mint time.
- Transport: the token is embedded in the `gag` remote URL
  (`https://agent:{token}@gag.{domain}/...`) or sent as
  `Authorization: Bearer {token}` for API calls. P0 accepts URL embedding;
  it is gate-only power, instantly revocable.
- Gate responses to a bad token mirror GitHub's `401` shape so git clients
  behave normally.
- Multiple tokens may exist (one per agent instance); each is audited by
  name.

## Do's and Don'ts

- Do store only hashes; the mint reply over Telegram is the single
  plaintext exposure, in the user's own chat.
- Do rate-limit token validation failures to slow brute force.
- Don't reuse GitHub PATs, GitHub App tokens, or any credential that
  resolves against github.com as an agent token.
- Don't build self-service enrollment endpoints in P0.

## Consequences

- Positive: minimal P0 code, no second server stack, instant revocation,
  per-agent attribution in the audit log.
- Trade-off: token visible in remote URLs and mint-chat — accepted; the
  token's power is bounded by the gate's policy engine and holds no GitHub
  authority whatsoever.
- Risk: a leaked agent token lets an attacker push *through the gate* —
  subject to policy (GATE-005), approvals (GATE-006), and the registry
  (GATE-010). Mitigation: revocation is one Telegram command; rulesets
  (backstop, see GATE-005 References) block the worst ops even so.

## Compliance and Enforcement

Review-verified: token store contains hashes only; every mux route except
`GET /`, the one-time setup form (nonce-gated), and health checks requires
a valid token; audit log records the token name, never the token.

## References

- GATE-002 (where the token lives), GATE-006 (mint/revoke commands),
  GATE-004 (the credential the agent must never see)

# GATE-004: Machine account credential custody — one classic PAT, held only by the gate

## Context

The agent acts on GitHub as a **machine account** — a dedicated GitHub user
account used only for automation. GitHub's Terms of Service explicitly allow
one free machine account per person; its actions are the creator's
responsibility. One identity covers all the user's repos and orgs; changing
access is a single role change that takes effect immediately.

Rejected alternatives (for the record):

- **GitHub App** (the previous design): permission edits need a manual
  settings change plus approval in every installed account; private Apps
  install only on their owning account, so multi-org coverage needs one App
  per org or a public App. Apps are built for products installed by many
  customers; for one person's agent the friction outweighs the benefits.
- **Fine-grained PAT**: cannot access repos where the account is only a
  collaborator on another user's *personal* account — which rules out the
  user's personal repos, the most common case. Org usage can also require
  org approval.
- **The gate holding the user's main-account token** so it could change
  roles itself: rejected — it would put the user's full GitHub power inside
  the gate; a bug or leak would expose everything. Role changes stay on
  GitHub, done by the user, guided by the gate (GATE-010/GATE-011).

## Decision

- **Credential:** one classic personal access token on the machine account,
  scopes `repo`, `workflow`, `read:org`. Classic tokens work everywhere the
  machine account has access, including collaborator seats on personal
  repos. Custom expiry ~6 months; the gate reminds at 14/3/1 days and runs
  `/rotate`.
- **Custody:** the token lives only in the gate. Encrypt at rest with
  AES-256-GCM; the encryption key comes from the environment
  (`GATE_TOKEN_ENC_KEY` in the stack `.env`) and is never stored with the
  ciphertext, in the database, or in backups of it. Decrypt only in memory,
  only in the request path. Never log the token or any `Authorization`
  header; scrub them from errors and stored GitHub responses.
- **Usage:** `Authorization: Bearer {token}` for REST/GraphQL;
  `Authorization: Basic base64("{machine_login}:{token}")` for git over
  HTTPS.
- **Verification** (intake, startup, daily, and `/rotate`):
  1. `GET /user` — `login` must equal the machine account username (a
     token from the main account is rejected with a pointed explanation);
     `two_factor_authentication` must be `true`; store `id` for commit
     identity.
  2. `X-OAuth-Scopes` must include all three scopes; report missing ones by
     name; warn on extras.
  3. `github-authentication-token-expiration` header stored; missing header
     (no expiry) is accepted with a warning.
- **Lifecycle:** `/rotate` mints a replacement with the old token live,
  verifies, swaps, then instructs deleting the old one on GitHub;
  `/disconnect` stops forwarding, erases the stored token, and instructs
  manual deletion. An expired/revoked token yields `credential_unavailable`
  to agents (GATE-010 error shapes) plus a rotation prompt.
- **Commit identity:** the agent's git environment sets author/committer to
  `{id}+{machine_login}@users.noreply.github.com` so GitHub links commits
  to the machine account profile and the private email never appears.
  Commit signing is out of scope for P0.
- The user keeps the machine account's password and 2FA secrets (password
  manager, recommended in setup); the gate never logs in to the GitHub
  website as the machine account.

## Do's and Don'ts

- Do treat the token as the crown jewel: one cipher, separate key, no logs,
  no echoes in errors.
- Do verify at startup; refuse to forward with an unverified credential.
- Don't widen scopes automatically when GitHub reports a scope gap — tell
  the user what's needed and let `/rotate` carry the decision.
- Don't store the machine account password anywhere; the gate has no
  interactive-login capability.

## Consequences

- Positive: classic PAT works across personal and org repos; blast radius
  is bounded by the machine account's roles; GitHub auto-revokes tokens
  leaked to public repos (gate then prompts `/rotate`).
- Trade-off: `repo` scope is broad, but every request still passes the
  policy engine (GATE-005) and registry (GATE-010); the credential cannot
  act outside the machine account's reach.
- Risk: token stolen from the gate. Mitigations: encryption with a
  separate key, no-log discipline, expiry + rotation, ruleset backstop on
  protected branches, and `/disconnect` for immediate shutdown.

## Compliance and Enforcement

Review-verified: AES-256-GCM at rest, key from env only, zero
token/Authorization occurrences in logs or stored responses (automated
grep in CI can check the audit JSONL). Startup refuses unverified tokens.

## References

- GATE-003 (what agents hold instead), GATE-010 (registry, errors),
  GATE-011 (guided setup incl. intake), GATE-006 (reminders, commands)

# GATE-005: Push classification and fail-closed policy

## Context

The threat model is a prompt-injected agent doing things the user never
asked: `git push --force`, branch deletion, repo-settings changes. The gate
must detect dangerous git operations before anything reaches GitHub, and
every undecided case must fail closed. Local bare mirrors (the git-proxy
approach) give local ancestry checks but cost storage and sync complexity.

## Decision

**Classification** — parse `git-receive-pack` pkt-lines to extract each
ref update `(old-oid, new-oid, refname)`:

- `new-oid` all-zeros → **branch-delete** or **tag-delete** (by ref
  namespace).
- `old-oid` all-zeros → create (treated as ordinary **push**).
- otherwise → **force-push** iff `old-oid` is not an ancestor of `new-oid`,
  checked via `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/compare/{old}...{new}`:
  `status: ahead` ⇒ fast-forward; `behind` or `diverged` ⇒ force; `404`
  (old tip unreachable) ⇒ **treat as force**; API failure ⇒ hold for
  approval (never assume safe).

**Policy** — a bind-mounted config file (global defaults + per-repo
overrides) maps each action class — `push`, `force-push`, `branch-delete`,
`tag-delete` — to `allow` | `approve` | `deny`. Defaults: `push: allow`;
`force-push`, `branch-delete`, `tag-delete: approve`. Reads (fetch,
upload-pack) pass through and are logged.

**Own-sphere vs third-party** (builder check settled): a repo is
*own-sphere* iff it has a registry entry (the user granted it, GATE-010)
or the machine account has an active membership in the owning org (only
possible via the user's invitation). Everything else is *third-party*.
Own-sphere repos follow the per-class policy above. **Mutations on
third-party repos always require approval in P0** — expected behavior
(contributing upstream: issues, PRs via fork), and the approval message is
how the user stays informed. Third-party private repos are unreachable
anyway (no access), so the rule is deterministic: registry-or-membership =
per-class policy; else mutations = approve.

**Approval semantics** — `approve` holds the operation; Telegram presents
repo, ref, old→new tips, and the commits being introduced (compare API's
`commits` list); approval is **one-shot for that exact operation** (repo +
ref + SHA pair). The agent's HTTP request waits; timeout (default 300 s) =
deny. A multi-ref push is held if any ref is non-`allow`; on approval the
push forwards exactly as received. Held requests bound the wait at the
approval timeout — role elevations (GATE-010) never extend it; a role gap
fails the request immediately with `permission_pending` and the agent
retries after the elevation completes.

**Kill switch** — Telegram `/block {owner}/{repo}` sets deny-all for that
repo (overrides config); `/unblock` restores. State persists in SQLite.

Anything not covered by config: deny (P0), never guess.

## Do's and Don'ts

- Do hold the full request until the decision; never forward-then-revert.
- Do verify classification inputs: malformed pkt-lines = hold, not pass.
- Don't extend an approval to a different SHA, ref, or repo.
- Don't add session unlocks ("force-push allowed for an hour") in P0 —
  explicit user decision; time-window rules are a post-P0 iteration.
- Don't treat `404`/`5xx` from the compare API as "safe".

## Consequences

- Positive: the two named harmful ops are impossible without a human tap;
  no local mirror infrastructure; classification needs only the compare API.
- Trade-off: an ancestry check per push costs one API call (rate limits:
  5,000/h on the machine token — fine for a single agent).
- Risk: policy file drift from reality. Mitigation: `/status` shows the
  effective policy per repo; config is re-read on change (mtime check).

## Compliance and Enforcement

Review-verified: every `receive-pack` path goes through classification;
tests cover zero-oid detection, compare-API mapping (ahead/behind/diverged/
404/error), timeout-deny, and one-shot scope; audit JSONL records decision,
basis (config rule vs approval vs kill switch), and approver.

## References

- GATE-006 (approval delivery), GATE-010 (role pre-flight after policy
  allows; grant-offer triggers; elevation fail-fast), GATE-001
  (ruleset backstop: protected branches block force-push/deletion
  server-side with the machine account excluded from bypass — deployed
  per `docs/guides/gitauthgate-setup.md` and noted in the post-setup
  Telegram message, GATE-011)

# GATE-006: Telegram is the P0 control channel

## Context

The user wants human-in-the-loop control with zero web-frontend surface in
P0: see what the agent is asking, approve/deny dangerous operations, mint
and revoke agent tokens, block repos, and be walked through GitHub
changes (GATE-011). Telegram inline keyboards deliver all of this without
building, hosting, or securing a web UI.

## Decision

A Telegram bot (long polling, no webhook URL needed) is the sole control
channel for P0.

**Security rules:**

- Allowlist of Telegram user IDs from config; messages from anyone else
  are ignored silently.
- State-changing buttons carry the flow's record ID plus a random value
  checked server-side, so stale, replayed, or forwarded buttons cannot
  trigger a different flow.
- No secrets are ever sent to Telegram. The single exception is the token
  paste fallback in setup (GATE-011 §5.2 step 7), which is deleted
  immediately via `deleteMessage`; failure to delete is surfaced to the
  user.
- Buttons act on live state: an approval for an already-expired or
  already-decided pending op replies with the current state, not a
  success.

**Message rules:** say what's happening, why, and exactly what to click
(GitHub's on-screen labels, bold, in link buttons); detect completion via
API instead of asking the user to confirm wherever possible; update
progress messages in place; end every flow with one summary.

**Commands:** `/status`, `/grant {owner}/{repo} [role]`, `/elevate
{owner}/{repo} {role}`, `/revoke {owner}/{repo}`, `/pending`, `/token
mint|revoke|list`, `/block|/unblock {owner}/{repo}`, `/rotate`,
`/disconnect`, `/setup`, plus inline Approve/Deny on held operations.

## Do's and Don'ts

- Do keep every flow resumable: durable records, `/pending` to list and
  resume/cancel.
- Do make approval messages show the operation's full shape (method, path,
  body for API; ref, tips, commit list for pushes).
- Don't send the GitHub PAT, agent tokens, or encryption keys to Telegram.
- Don't build a web dashboard in P0 (explicit scope cut; post-P0).

## Consequences

- Positive: approvals reach the user's phone; no web stack to build;
  setup, elevation, and token life all ride one channel.
- Trade-off: single control channel — if Telegram is down, approvals wait
  (and time out as denies, per GATE-005). Accepted: fail-closed is the
  design's posture.
- Risk: Telegram chat compromise. Mitigations: allowlist, signed buttons,
  no secrets policy; the worst leak is visibility into operations, not
  credentials.

## Compliance and Enforcement

Review-verified: allowlist enforced on every update; button callbacks
validated against live records; a CI grep asserts no secret-bearing
strings in outbound Telegram payloads (tokens are hashed/masked at log and
send sites).

## References

- GATE-005 (what approvals look like), GATE-010 (grant/elevation flows),
  GATE-011 (setup walkthrough), GATE-003 (token mint/revoke)

# GATE-007: GitHub API proxy surface — `/api/v3` with held mutations

## Context

The user wants *every* agent action behind the gate — not just git. The
GitHub API surface is huge, so the gate cannot hand-write policy per
endpoint; it needs a small, uniform rule plus structured visibility. Stock
tools must work unmodified: `gh` and other clients speak GitHub-Enterprise
style `/api/v3` on a configurable host.

## Decision

The gate exposes `https://gag.{domain}/api/v3/*` and translates to
`https://api.github.com/` with the machine token injected.

- **GET (reads):** pass through, log method/path/status in the audit.
  GraphQL *queries* are POSTs — `POST /api/v3/graphql` is inspected: if
  the body contains no `mutation`, treat as a read; if it does, treat as a
  mutation.
- **Non-GET (mutations):** held. Telegram presents method, path, and body
  (JSON pretty-printed; issue/PR bodies are human-readable by design).
  Forwarded verbatim on approval; request fails closed on timeout/denial.
- **Agent wiring:** `GH_HOST=gag.{domain}`,
  `GITHUB_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN={agent token}` for `gh`; base-URL override for
  other clients. Exact `gh` env behavior is confirmed by the M1 spike.
  These vars are set only when the `gag` profile is enabled, so opt-out
  degrades cleanly (GATE-001).
- **Policy interaction:** after policy `allow`/approval (GATE-005), the
  access layer runs role pre-flight (GATE-010) before forwarding.
- **Agent-facing errors** use fixed shapes (defined in GATE-010) so agents
  can react programmatically; GitHub's own permission errors map per the
  error-handling table (404 = access removed, 403 + "admin rights" = role
  gap → elevation, 403 + `X-Accepted-OAuth-Scopes` gap = scope decision
  for the user, 401 = credential dead → `/rotate` prompt).
- `GET /proxy/elevations/{id}` lets an agent poll elevation state.

## Do's and Don'ts

- Do forward the request body byte-for-byte after approval; never modify
  semantics.
- Do cap the size of bodies echoed to Telegram (truncate with a pointer to
  the full body in the audit log).
- Don't parse or whitelist individual endpoints in P0; uniform mutation
  policy now, action families later.
- Don't leak the injected credential into error bodies or audit entries.

## Consequences

- Positive: complete coverage of agent activity with one rule; stock tool
  compatibility; bodies on approval messages give the user exactly the
  "verify the command matches expectations" moment they asked for.
- Trade-off: every mutation waits on a human tap in P0 — deliberately
  annoying until time-window rules land (post-P0, explicit user plan).
- Risk: huge bodies slow the hold path. Mitigation: size cap + audit
  reference; timeouts keep requests from hanging forever.

## Compliance and Enforcement

Review-verified: GET passthrough never runs a mutation test incorrectly
(GraphQL body scan has tests); held requests forward byte-identical on
approval; no Authorization header appears in audit entries.

## References

- GATE-005 (policy layer feeds this), GATE-010 (pre-flight + errors),
  GATE-006 (approval messages), GATE-002 (agent env wiring principle)

# GATE-008: Platform trait — GitHub adapter only in P0

## Context

GitLab and Bitbucket support is a future requirement, but building two
adapters at once triples P0 surface. The platform-specific facts are small
and enumerable: the upstream git remote URL shape, the ancestry/compare
check, and the API base + auth style.

## Decision

Internally, everything platform-specific sits behind one trait:

```
trait Platform {
    fn git_upstream_url(&self, owner: &str, repo: &str) -> Url;   // where pushes/fetches go
    fn is_ancestor(&self, owner: &str, repo: &str, old: &Oid, new: &Oid) -> Ancestry;  // FF? force? unknown?
    fn api_base(&self) -> Url;                                    // where /api/v3 maps to
    fn apply_auth(&self, req: &mut Request, token: &MachineToken);
    fn role_of(&self, permissions: &PermissionsObj) -> Role;      // registry mapping
}
```

P0 ships the **GitHub adapter only** (compare API for ancestry, Basic/Bearer
auth, `permissions`-object role mapping). GitLab (`/api/v4`, its compare
endpoint) and Bitbucket slot in later behind the same trait. External URL
scheme stays `gag.{host}/git/{owner}/{repo}.git` for GitHub in P0; when a
second platform lands, paths dispatch per platform (`/git/{owner}/...` vs
prefixed or per-host variants) — a one-line change in the instruction page
(GATE-002), not a protocol change.

## Do's and Don'ts

- Do route all classification (GATE-005) and registry checks (GATE-010)
  through the trait, never call `api.github.com` from shared code.
- Do give `is_ancestor` an explicit `unknown` state — adapters must map
  API failures to `unknown`, and policy treats `unknown` as hold (fail
  closed).
- Don't stub or half-build GitLab/Bitbucket code paths in P0.
- Don't let platform assumptions (e.g., `diverged` enum strings) leak out
  of the adapter.

## Consequences

- Positive: P0 stays single-platform; multi-platform later is an adapter +
  URL-scheme decision, not a rewrite.
- Trade-off: one layer of indirection around every upstream call — trivial
  cost.
- Risk: trait shaped wrong for a future platform (e.g., Bitbucket Cloud's
  sparse compare support). Mitigation: the `unknown` escape hatch keeps
  policy safe with any adapter.

## Compliance and Enforcement

Review-verified: `github.com`/`api.github.com` literals appear only inside
the GitHub adapter module; policy code consumes `Ancestry`/`Role`, never
raw upstream responses.

## References

- GATE-005 (classification consumes the trait), GATE-010 (registry roles),
  GATE-007 (API base mapping)

# GATE-009: Build, image, and configuration

## Context

Codery builds tool images on-host (no registry CI): `docker build -t
codery-gate:<date> images/gate`, then point `GATE_IMAGE` at the tag and
Deploy. The gate needs no git binary — it streams git smart-HTTP bytes,
parses pkt-lines, and calls upstream HTTP APIs.

## Decision

- **Language:** Rust (project preference order; confirmed with the user).
  Single binary: axum (HTTP server), reqwest (upstream client), tokio
  (tasks: Telegram long-poll, registry re-checks, expiry reminders, daily
  token verification), rusqlite (state), serde/serde_json.
- **Image:** small static build (musl or distroless-style); no git, no
  shell dependencies at runtime.
- **Stack `.env` keys** (all documented in `host/templates/env.example`):
  - `GATE_IMAGE` — image tag
  - `GATE_PUBLIC_URL` — e.g. `https://gag.{domain}` (one-time form links,
    instruction page content)
  - `GATE_TOKEN_ENC_KEY` — AES-256-GCM key for token-at-rest encryption
    (never co-located with ciphertext; GATE-004)
  - `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`, `TELEGRAM_ALLOWLIST` — control channel
    (GATE-006)
  - `DOMAIN_NAME` — already in the stack env
- **State layout** (bind mount `/opt/codery/data/gate`): SQLite DB
  (registry, flows, setup progress, pending approvals, kill-switch state,
  hashed agent tokens) + append-only audit JSONL. Both restart-resilient;
  setup and elevation flows resume from durable records (GATE-011/GATE-010).
- **Policy config:** bind-mounted file (e.g. `/opt/codery/data/gate/
  policy.toml`), re-read on mtime change; effective policy visible via
  `/status` (GATE-005).
- **Testing:** integration tests run a real `git` client against the gate
  with a stub upstream (bare repo + wiremock); the approval backend sits
  behind a trait so tests use an auto-approve/auto-deny stub; Telegram is
  never contacted in CI.

## Do's and Don'ts

- Do keep the service single-binary and stateless except for the bind
  mount — recreating the container must lose nothing.
- Do derive all URLs from `GATE_PUBLIC_URL`/`DOMAIN_NAME`; no hardcoded
  hostnames.
- Don't publish host ports beyond loopback (GATE-001).
- Don't add a web UI, metrics stack, or admin panel in P0.

## Consequences

- Positive: cheap on-host builds; the whole system is one binary + SQLite
  + JSONL + two env secrets; recreates are safe.
- Trade-off: SQLite over Postgres — right-sized for one instance, one
  user; a multi-tenant future would revisit (unlikely for Codery tools).
- Risk: bind-mount permission drift. Mitigation: container runs with a
  fixed UID/GID documented in the compose service comments, matching
  other tools' data-dir conventions.

## Compliance and Enforcement

Review-verified: image builds via the documented command; no runtime
dependencies beyond the static binary; `.env` keys match this list exactly.

- GATE-001 (placement), GATE-004 (encryption key discipline), GATE-005

# GATE-010: Access registry, granting, and elevation

## Context

The machine account's power on GitHub is exactly its roles per repo. The
user changes roles on GitHub (the gate never holds the user's own
credentials); the gate's job is to know the current state, tell the user
exactly where to click when more access is needed, verify the change took
effect, and hand agents structured errors they can react to.

## Decision

**Registry** (SQLite, per repo):

```
owner/repo
granted_role     // what GitHub reports: admin|maintain|write|triage|read|none
intended_role    // what the user wants (usually write)
via              // collaborator | org_team | org_member
last_verified_at
```

Actual role comes from `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}` `permissions` object
(`admin/maintain/push/triage/pull` → highest true = role); `404` = no
access. Re-check every 30 minutes, every 5 seconds during a grant or
elevation flow. Unexpected role drops update the registry and notify the
user as a short notice — never ask them to undo it.

**Granting** (`/grant`, setup step 8, or an offered grant): instructions
differ for personal repos (no role choice; collaborator ≈ Write) and org
repos (role menu; outside collaborator); one link button to the
collaborator settings page. The gate accepts the invitation
automatically: poll `GET /user/repository_invitations` every 5 s,
`PATCH /user/repository_invitations/{id}`; one reminder after 1 h;
invitations expire after 7 days (re-invite). Confirm via `GET
/repos/...` until permissions match, update registry + checklist message;
if the user picked a lower role, say exactly what's wrong and where to
fix it. Mention paid-plan seat usage once per org.

**Grant-offer trigger** (builder check settled): only mutations trigger
it, only when pre-flight finds the machine account has **no access** to
the repo (`GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}` → `404`, which GitHub returns for
both "doesn't exist" and "private, no access" — indistinguishable), and
only once per repo per 24 h (debounced). A mutation on a public repo the
machine account *can* reach is third-party (GATE-005: approval flow,
never a grant offer); reads never trigger offers — unregistered reads
forward upstream and pass through whatever GitHub says, without Telegram
noise.

**Role map:** action type → minimum role (Read for reads; Triage for
label/assign; Write for push/PR-merge/release/workflow files; Maintain for
topics/Pages; Admin for settings/rulesets/collaborators/delete), built
from GitHub's repository-roles documentation. Used for pre-flight before
forwarding; a GitHub rejection contradicting the map is logged for map
correction.

**Elevation:** triggered by pre-flight role gap (preferred), a GitHub 403
role error, or `/elevate`. Collect gaps for ~10 s before asking, present
together. State machine (durable in SQLite):

```
DETECTED → AWAITING_USER_CONSENT → AWAITING_ROLE_CHANGE → VERIFYING → DONE
any → CANCELLED | EXPIRED (24 h no progress)
```

- Consent message: why, needed role, current role, one line on what the
  new role adds; buttons `[Grant it] [Grant until done, then remove] [Not
  now]`.
- Role-change message: exact clicks, link button; `via: org_team` points
  at the team page and warns it affects the whole team.
- VERIFYING: poll every 5 s; wrong role → say what it is vs needed;
  10 min silence → one reminder.
- **Temporary elevation** auto-triggers reduction (back to intended role)
  once the triggering request succeeds.
- Personal repos have no Maintain/Admin for collaborators →
  `role_unavailable` + DIY instructions for the user; suggest moving the
  repo to an org if it happens often.

**Reduction/removal** (`/revoke`, temporary-elevation completion,
`/disconnect`): instructions + verification (`404` = fully removed),
registry updated.

**Agent-facing errors** (fixed JSON shapes):
`access_pending`, `permission_pending` (with `elevation_id`,
`needs_role`), `role_unavailable`, `credential_unavailable` — plus
`GET /proxy/elevations/{id}` for polling. GitHub error mapping: 404 =
access removed (re-check + notify), 403 "must have admin rights" = role
gap → elevation, 403 scope header gap = user decides via `/rotate`, 401 =
`credential_unavailable` + rotation prompt.

## Do's and Don'ts

- Do run the full grant/elevation conversation on Telegram; the agent
  never sees GitHub's settings pages.
- Do keep every flow record durable and resumable after restart; resend a
  step only if it is >1 h old.
- Don't retry an elevated action without confirming the registry moved.
- Don't silently widen anything: every role change originates from the
  user's GitHub click.

## Consequences

- Positive: the agent requests access like a colleague would; the user
  makes every access decision on GitHub with exact instructions; roles
  self-heal (30-min re-checks) without user maintenance.
- Trade-off: an action needing more role **fails immediately** with
  `permission_pending` (+ `elevation_id`) — requests never hang on a role
  change (role changes routinely exceed any reasonable HTTP hold); the
  agent backs off, polls `GET /proxy/elevations/{id}`, and retries after
  DONE. Only approval-holds (GATE-005, bounded by the approval timeout)
  ever wait on a human.
- Risk: role map drift vs GitHub reality. Mitigation: contradictions are
  logged with method/path for map fixes.

## Compliance and Enforcement

Review-verified: state-machine transitions have unit tests incl. restart
resume; polling intervals match this ADR; audit JSONL records each
elevation (trigger, role, duration, outcome) and temporary reductions.

## References

- GATE-004 (why the gate can't change roles itself), GATE-006 (message
  rules, commands), GATE-007 (error surface + elevations endpoint),
  GATE-011 (first-time setup uses the same grant machinery)

# GATE-011: Guided Telegram setup

## Context

Setup involves a dozen GitHub settings pages (account creation, 2FA,
token creation, collaborator invites). The user should never have to work
out GitHub's UI alone; the gate walks them through every step over
Telegram, verifies what it can via the API, and never takes over the
browser. The walkthrough runs on first start with no token configured,
and re-runs per-step whenever something is missing later (deleted token,
2FA off, `/setup`).

## Decision

**The eight steps:**

0. **Introduction** — what a machine account is, ~10 min estimate,
   `[Start]`.
1. **Email** — plus-address alias of the user's email (suggested, not
   stored after setup); fallback: any address they can receive.
2. **Sign-up** — private/incognito window; username clearly tied to the
   user (e.g. `rob-agent`); password into a password manager; gate
   verifies the username exists via unauthenticated
   `GET /users/{username}` and waits; suggests alternatives if taken.
3. **Profile** — name/bio marking the account as automated, operated by
   the main account.
4. **Private email** — check **Keep my email addresses private** and
   **Block command line pushes that expose my email**.
5. **2FA** — enable, save recovery codes with the password; confirmed
   later via `GET /user` `two_factor_authentication`.
6. **Token** — prefilled link
   `https://github.com/settings/tokens/new?scopes=repo,workflow,read:org&description=GitHub%20agent%20proxy`;
   custom expiry ~6 months; gate promises 14/3/1-day reminders.
7. **Token intake** — preferred: one-time HTTPS form
   `{GATE_PUBLIC_URL}/setup/token?nonce=...` (single-use nonce, 15 min
   expiry, one password field); fallback without a public URL: paste in
   Telegram, message deleted instantly via `deleteMessage` (failure told
   to the user). Then full verification per GATE-004 §6.3 — a token from
   the main account is rejected by name with the fix ("create it signed
   in as **rob-agent** in the private window") and returns to step 6.
8. **Repo access** — user sends `owner/repo` names; each runs the grant
   flow (GATE-010) as an in-place checklist; finish message summarizes
   reachable repos and lists commands, and includes the **ruleset
   backstop** reminder (protected branches with force-push/deletion
   blocked, machine account excluded from bypass — full walkthrough in
   `docs/guides/gitauthgate-setup.md`).

**Rules for every step:** one step per message — what, why, exactly what
to click (GitHub's labels, bold); one link button, prefilled where GitHub
allows; the gate auto-detects completion where the API allows (username
exists, 2FA flag, role change) — the user never types "done" except steps
1–5 which carry a `[Done]` button; every step has `[I'm stuck]` (resends
with more detail + common problems) and `[Cancel setup]`; progress is
durable and resumes at the same step after restart; a step older than 1 h
on resume is resent.

## Do's and Don'ts

- Do keep the machine account's password/2FA entirely on the user's side;
  say so plainly in the walkthrough.
- Do prefer the one-time form whenever `GATE_PUBLIC_URL` is set.
- Don't proceed past step 7 without full token verification.
- Don't store the user's main email beyond the alias suggestion.

## Consequences

- Positive: a first-time user reaches a working agent in one repo using
  only Telegram-guided steps (acceptance test); setup re-runs for any
  missing piece without a rebuild or `.env` edit.
- Trade-off: the walkthrough is stateful code (durable progress, per-step
  reruns) — accepted; it replaces every manual config document.
- Risk: GitHub UI label drift. Mitigation: labels are data (step
  definitions), reviewable and updatable without touching flow logic;
  `[I'm stuck]` catches the gap in the moment.

## Compliance and Enforcement

Review-verified: steps and copy match this ADR; nonce single-use +
expiring; paste-fallback deletion is tested; the acceptance checklist
(lives in the implementation plan: first-run to working agent in one repo
via Telegram only; wrong-account token rejected with a pointed
explanation; role-change detection without user confirmation; "grant
until done then remove"; expiry reminders at 14/3/1 days; zero
token/Authorization strings in logs) is an explicit manual QA gate before
release.

## References

- GATE-004 (verification, custody), GATE-006 (message/security rules),
  GATE-010 (grant machinery in step 8), GATE-009 (`GATE_PUBLIC_URL`)
